extracted.intended_audience: students and practitioners of social psychology, political leaders, orators, and anyone studying mass persuasion
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines and theoretical criteria about how crowds form opinions and how leaders and rhetorical techniques (affirmation, repetition, contagion, prestige) act on masses. Focuses on the psychology of crowds, leader types, and means of influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illusions as the chief factor in mass evolution
rubrics_metrics.description: Not truth, but error has always been the chief factor in the evolution of nations; masses prefer illusions and turn instinctively to rhetoricians who accord them what they want.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illusions supply 'hope and illusion without which they cannot live' and are championed by minds willing to promise happiness (example: socialism as 'the last illusion that is still vital'). Destroying illusions dries up hope and often requires terrible disturbances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experience as the effective process to establish truth
rubrics_metrics.description: Experience constitutes almost the only effective process by which a truth may be solidly established in the mind of the masses; experiences must be on a very large scale and very frequently repeated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Historical facts are usually ineffective across generations; only large-scale, repeated experiential catastrophes or trials (e.g., French Revolution, wars, long periods of disastrous Protection) will shake deeply implanted erroneous opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: The negative value of reason on crowds
rubrics_metrics.description: Crowds are not to be influenced by reasoning and can only comprehend rough-and-ready associations of ideas; the laws of logic have no action on crowds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Orators who influence crowds appeal to sentiments, not reason. Prepared, studied harangues fail because the orator follows his own line rather than the hearers'. To influence crowds one must 'pretend to share these sentiments' and vary language according to instant effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of a leader: instinctive obedience and organization
rubrics_metrics.description: As soon as beings are gathered they place themselves under the authority of a chief; the leader's will is the nucleus around which opinions of the crowd are grouped and attain identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Leaders may be mere ringleaders or agitators but they organise heterogeneous crowds and pave the way for sects; a crowd is 'a servile flock' that needs a master.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leader origin and hypnotisation by an idea
rubrics_metrics.description: The leader has most often started as one of the led and has himself been hypnotised by the idea whose apostle he becomes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such leaders have the idea take possession of them so entirely that contrary opinions vanish; example: Robespierre hypnotised by Rousseau's ideas and using Inquisition methods to propagate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Leader temperament and sacrifice
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders are more frequently men of action than thinkers: morbidly nervous, excitable, bordering on madness; they sacrifice personal interest and are often indifferent to contempt and persecution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Their intensity of faith gives great power of suggestion; the multitude listens to the strong-willed man because individuals in crowds lose force of will and turn to whoever possesses it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two classes of leaders: intermittent energy vs enduring will
rubrics_metrics.description: Ringleaders divide into (1) energetic men possessing intermittent strength of will (useful for sudden enterprises) and (2) rarer men of enduring strength of will (true founders of religions and great undertakings).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Energetic leaders (Ney, Murat, Garibaldi) are brilliant but transitory and often weak in ordinary life; enduring-will leaders (St. Paul, Mahomet, Columbus, de Lesseps) exert far greater, lasting influence and 'the world belongs to them.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Leaders' despotic authority and usurpation of public power
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaders of crowds wield a very despotic authority and can extort obedience even without formal backing; they may usurp the place of public authorities as those authorities weaken.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This despotism explains how leaders can fix labour hours, decree strikes, and how removing leaders (e.g., arrest) can dissolve movements; crowds seek servitude more than liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of action: affirmation (simple, concise assertion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affirmation pure and simple, kept free of all reasoning and all proof, is one of the surest means of making an idea enter the mind of crowds.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The more concise and free of proof the affirmation, the more weight it carries; religious books, legal codes, statesmen and advertisers use simple affirmation to instil beliefs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of action: repetition (same terms, embedding in unconscious)
rubrics_metrics.description: Affirmation has no real influence unless constantly repeated, and so far as possible in the same terms; repetition fixes a statement in the mind until it is accepted as truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Repeated statements embed in 'profound regions of our unconscious' and we forget the author and accept the assertion (examples: advertising claims, repeated press slanders or praises). Repetition combats contrary repetition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Means of action: contagion (emotional and ideational spread)
rubrics_metrics.description: When an affirmation has been sufficiently repeated and there is unanimity, a current of opinion is formed and contagion intervenes; ideas, sentiments, emotions, and beliefs possess in crowds a contagious power as intense as microbes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contagion explains sudden panics and mass imitation; it can act at a distance (e.g., revolutionary movements spreading between countries) and forces individuals to adopt modes of feeling as well as ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Imitation as an effect of contagion
rubrics_metrics.description: Imitation is not an independent cause but a mere effect of contagion; man has a natural tendency to imitation provided it is easy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fashion and social conformity spread by simple, easy imitation; highly superior innovators fail to influence if their ideas are too far from received opinions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preparedness and prestige required for rapid suggestion
rubrics_metrics.description: To stir up a crowd for short-term action (pillaging, defending a barricade, etc.) rapid suggestion and example are most powerful, but the crowd must be previously prepared and the agent must possess 'prestige.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example and rapid suggestion work best when circumstances prepare the crowd; prestige is the leader-quality that enables such rapid influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prestige: domination that paralyses critical faculty
rubrics_metrics.description: Prestige is a sort of domination exercised on our mind by an individual, a work, or an idea that entirely paralyses our critical faculty and fills the soul with astonishment and respect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prestige prevents seeing things as they are; it is the mainspring of all authority—neither gods, kings, nor women have reigned without it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of prestige: acquired (artificial) vs personal
rubrics_metrics.description: Prestige divides into acquired (resulting from name, fortune, reputation, titles, uniforms) and personal (peculiar to the individual's personality); acquired prestige is most common but personal prestige can exist without reputation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Acquired prestige (uniforms, titles) can confer authority regardless of personal worth (examples: soldiers in uniform, judges' robes); prestige of opinions/works often arises from accumulated repetition and historical authority (examples: Homer, the Parthenon).

rubrics_metrics.name: Contagion's capacity to carry false or deformed ideas back to elites
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas that originate in higher thought can be distorted by leaders and agitators, propagated among masses by affirmation/repetition/contagion, and then return to influence higher social strata in deformed form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The process explains how philosophers' ideas may triumph indirectly long after their deaths, transformed by popular propagation; contagion thus shapes destiny indirectly rather than by direct intellectual reasoning.
